Front: In this series circuit, what happens if bulb A breaks?
Back: Both bulbs go out.
Extra cue: A series circuit has only one path for current.
Choices: Both bulbs go out.|Only bulb A goes out.|Only bulb B gets brighter.|The battery becomes neutral.

Front: In this parallel circuit, what happens if bulb A breaks?
Back: Bulb B can stay on.
Extra cue: A parallel circuit has more than one path for current.
Choices: Bulb B can stay on.|Both bulbs must go out.|Current stops everywhere.|The voltage becomes zero.

Front: Why is the ammeter labelled A placed like this?
Back: It is in series, so it measures the current through the circuit.
Extra cue: Ammeters must be connected in series.
Choices: It is in series, so it measures the current through the circuit.|It is in parallel, so it measures voltage.|It is used to test pH.|It makes the bulb brighter.

Front: Why is the voltmeter labelled A connected like this?
Back: It is in parallel across the lamp, so it measures voltage across the lamp.
Extra cue: Voltmeters measure potential difference across a component.
Choices: It is in parallel across the lamp, so it measures voltage across the lamp.|It is in series to measure current.|It replaces the battery.|It measures pH.

Front: What is wrong with this circuit?
Back: The voltmeter is connected in series instead of parallel.
Extra cue: Voltmeters should go across a component, not in the main loop.
Choices: The voltmeter is connected in series instead of parallel.|The lamp is missing a filament.|The battery is made from two bulbs.|The switch is closed.

Front: For the AND switch circuit, what must happen for the lamp to light?
Back: Both switches A and B must be closed.
Extra cue: AND means A and B together.
Choices: Both switches A and B must be closed.|Either A or B can be closed.|Only switch A matters.|The pH must be 7.

Front: For the OR switch circuit, what must happen for the lamp to light?
Back: Either switch A or switch B can be closed.
Extra cue: OR means this switch or that switch.
Choices: Either switch A or switch B can be closed.|Both switches must always be open.|Both switches must be closed together.|The bulb must be in acid.

Front: The switch labelled A is open. What does this do?
Back: It breaks the circuit so the lamp is off.
Extra cue: Open means there is a gap.
Choices: It breaks the circuit so the lamp is off.|It makes current bigger.|It changes acid to alkali.|It measures voltage.

Front: What do the arrows labelled A show?
Back: The direction of conventional current around the circuit.
Extra cue: Current flows when there is a complete circuit.
Choices: The direction of conventional current around the circuit.|The direction of breathing.|The pH scale direction.|The movement of cartilage.

Front: What is wrong with this circuit?
Back: There is a short path that bypasses the lamp.

Choices: There is a short path that bypasses the lamp.|The lamp is in parallel correctly.|The voltmeter is measuring pH.|The switch is open.

Front: On the pH scale, which label shows an acid?

Front: In the universal indicator colours, which label is most acidic?

Back: Indicator.

Front: In the neutralisation setup, what reaction is being tested?
Back: Acid + alkali → salt + water.

Front: What is the purpose of heating the solution in an evaporation dish?
Back: To evaporate water and leave salt crystals.

Front: What is the main safety mistake in the diagram?
Back: Acid is being poured without clear eye protection.
Extra cue: Acid practicals need goggles and careful handling.
Choices: Acid is being poured without clear eye protection.|The beaker is made of glass.|The liquid is below pH 7.|The student is using indicator.

Front: What is wrong with this indicator method?
Back: Too much indicator has been added.
Extra cue: Usually only a few drops of indicator are needed.
Choices: Too much indicator has been added.|The beaker should be a battery.|Indicator should never change colour.|The acid has become a muscle.

Front: What is the safer way to dilute acid?
Back: Add acid slowly to water.
Extra cue: Use care: acid into water, slowly, with goggles.
Choices: Add acid slowly to water.|Add water quickly to concentrated acid.|Use no eye protection.|Heat it until it splashes.

Front: Why should you add alkali slowly during neutralisation?
Back: To avoid overshooting the neutral point.
Extra cue: Adding too much can make the solution alkaline instead of neutral.
Choices: To avoid overshooting the neutral point.|To make the bulb brighter.|To stop muscles contracting.|To make current flow backwards.

Front: A student says: “pH 1 is a strong alkali.” What is wrong?
Back: pH 1 is a strong acid.
Extra cue: Low pH means acidic, high pH means alkaline.
Choices: pH 1 is a strong acid.|pH 1 is neutral.|pH 1 is the strongest alkali.|pH only applies to electricity.

Front: In the elbow joint diagram, which label shows cartilage?

Front: In the elbow joint diagram, which label shows a ligament?
Back: B

Back: One contracts while the other relaxes to move the bone in opposite directions.

Choices: A|B|C|None of them
